Case-control study. Forty-four Arabian horses (24 stallions, 20 mares) were enrolled as lame (n = 23), non-lame (n = 11), and control (n = 10). Field-based grouping was determined by veterinary-gate assessment: horses eliminated for irregular gait were classified as lame, and finishers passing veterinary inspection as non-lame. Blinded trot-up videos were reviewed to verify grouping and assign AAEP lameness grades; facial expression videos recorded at the veterinary gate were used to assess facial action units. Blood analyses measured biochemical markers. Real-time PCR quantified serum miR-21 and miR-155. Facial expression scales had high area under the curve values for distinguishing lame from non-lame horses (HGS: 0.947, 95% CI: 0.850-1.000; EQUUS-FAP: 0.917, 95% CI: 0.817-1.000). Facial scores were strongly correlated with AAEP lameness grades (r ≈ 0.78, p ≤ 0.001). Lame horses had higher oxidative stress index, lactate, lactate dehydrogenase, cortisol, aspartate aminotransferase concentrations, and miR-21 expression than other groups (p ≤ 0.015). The small sample size warrants confirmation of the results in larger populations. Facial expression scores were associated with AAEP lameness grades and selected biochemical and molecular parameters in endurance horses. Facial expression assessment may provide complementary information alongside established lameness evaluation methods. Further studies are needed to confirm its role in pain-related lameness assessment.

title: Embracing the Dragon-Horse Spirit: Gratitude and forward momentum.
abstract: Dragon-Horse Spirit: A metaphor for a person's vigorous and enterprising spirit and demeanor. Inspired by this spirit, iMeta and its sister journals have achieved a series of groundbreaking advancements in submission and impact over the past 4 years. title: Uncovering cardiac molecular remodelling in racing Thoroughbreds with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common arrhythmia in both humans and horses, with a comparable prevalence of ~2%. In horses, AF is a major cause of poor athletic performance and linked to sudden cardiac death, yet its underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. To investigate transcriptomic remodelling associated with spontaneous paroxysmal AF (PAF). Case-control study. We performed RNA sequencing on left atrial (LA) tissue from three Thoroughbred racehorses with PAF and four matched controls. All horses were euthanised due to musculoskeletal reasons. Cell type deconvolution was performed with BayesPrism. The differential expression analysis was performed with EdgeR. Alternative splicing analysis was performed with SUPPA2. Cell-type deconvolution revealed a modest, non-significant shift towards increased fibroblast and immune cell proportions in PAF, but not enough to account for widespread transcriptional changes. 1400 of the 12,012 included genes were considered significantly differentially expressed (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value <0.05). These genes included ion channels, calcium-handling proteins, and conduction-related genes. In addition, several genes directly involved in cardiac muscle contraction and mitochondrial energy metabolism were differentially expressed. Alternative splicing analysis revealed over 20 significantly altered events, including skipped exons in genes with potential relevance to cardiac function and remodelling. The number of biological replicates was modest. Overall, despite no major changes in cell composition, the findings highlight intrinsic structural and molecular changes in the LA of PAF-affected horses. This study provides the first transcriptomic and splicing analysis of atrial tissue in racehorses with PAF, revealing molecular remodelling consistent with mechanisms of arrhythmia maintenance and suggesting potential targets for further functional investigation.

title: Harnessing CSC recruitment: photo-triggered "self-exploding" macrophages for targeted metastasis inhibition.
abstract: Cancer metastasis is a serious threat to human health. Cancer stem cells (CSC) are closely related to tumor metastasis, but it is difficult to achieve accurate drug delivery and effective inhibition of CSC due to the complex tumor microenvironment. Herein, we report a living cell delivery system, C-H@M2, engineered by loading M2 macrophages with carrier-free Ce6/Honokiol self-assembled nanoparticles. This system is designed to harness the tumor's intrinsic recruitment mechanism for targeted anti-metastasis therapy. Acting as a "Trojan Horse", C-H@M2 exploits the active recruitment of M2 macrophages by CSC to achieve precise tumor homing. Upon laser irradiation, the macrophages undergo photo-triggered immunogenic lysis ("self-explosion"), leading to the burst release of therapeutic payloads and the induction of robust immunogenic cell death (ICD). HK as an inhibitor of Forkhead box M1 (FOXM1) inhibits CSC stemness and epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT) in tumor tissues. In vivo experimental results demonstrate that C-H@M2 significantly inhibits tumor and lung metastasis through a triple-modal strategy: Self-explosion enhanced ICD effect, stemness and EMT inhibition, CSC killing by stemness inhibition and PDT. Our study provides a novel strategy for CSC targeted therapy and cancer metastasis inhibition.

title: Infection and abduction loss predict equine laryngoplasty failure.
abstract: Prosthetic laryngoplasty (PL) is the most common surgical treatment for recurrent laryngeal neuropathy (RLN) in horses. Post-operative complications may compromise outcomes, and the influence of breed and anaesthetic approach remains unclear. To evaluate factors associated with surgical outcome at 3 months following PL, focusing on post-operative complications, anaesthetic modality and breed (particularly Iberian baroque breeds). Multicentre retrospective cohort study. Medical records from 181 horses across 7 equine hospitals using the same standardised surgical technique were reviewed. Variables including breed, anaesthesia type, ventriculocordectomy (VeC) method and post-operative complications were analysed using χ2 or Fisher's exact tests and Spearman correlation. Two binomial generalised linear mixed models, with surgeon as a random effect, evaluated pre/intra-operative predictors and post-operative prognostic factors. Level of significance p < 0.05. Surgical success was defined as the absence of respiratory noise and exercise intolerance at 3 months. Surgical success was achieved in 79.1% of cases. Complications occurred in 33.7% of horses and were negatively associated with treatment success (odds ratio [OR] 0.003; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.000-0.052; p < 0.001). Major loss of arytenoid abduction (18.2%) and surgical site infection (SSI; 6.6%) were the only variables independently associated with reduced odds of treatment success in the post-operative model (OR 0.011; 95% CI 0.001-0.178; p = 0.001 and OR 0.046; 95% CI 0.004-0.559; p = 0.016, respectively). Breed was not associated with surgical outcome. The retrospective multicentre design may introduce selection bias, variability in clinical practice and heterogeneous follow-up. Major loss of arytenoid abduction and SSI were the strongest predictors of failure, highlighting the importance of meticulous technique, preservation of arytenoid abduction and rigorous infection control to optimise outcomes after PL.

title: The genome sequence of horse-radish, Armoracia rusticana G.Gaertn., B.Mey. & Scherb. (Brassicales: Brassicaceae).
abstract: We present a genome assembly of Armoracia rusticana (horse-radish; Streptophyta; Magnoliopsida; Brassicales; Brassicaceae). The assembly consists of two haplotypes with total lengths of 605.90 megabases and 589.75 megabases. The haplotype 1 assembly and the haplotype 2 assembly each contain 16 chromosomal pseudomolecules; these account for 99.56% and 99.22% of their respective sequences. The mitochondrial genome assembly has a length of 316.39 kilobases and the plastid genome assemblies have lengths of 156.67 and 155.14 kilobases. Gene annotation of the haplotype 1 assembly by Ensembl identified 40,675 protein-coding genes. This assembly was generated as part of the Darwin Tree of Life project, which produces reference genomes for eukaryotic species found in Britain and Ireland.
